title: The Signs of the Art: Planets, Zodiac, Elements and Alchemical Characters
family: Not an alphabet. The shorthand signs (notae) of astronomy, astrology and alchemy, with the sixteen dot figures of geomancy. They stand for things, not sounds.
summary: Not an alphabet but the shorthand of the heavens and the laboratory. Secondary summaries of Alexander Jones's edition of the Oxyrhynchus astronomical papyri (1999) read the Saturn and Jupiter signs as monograms of the Greek names Κρόνος and Ζεύς and the Mercury sign as a stylised caduceus; the origin of the Mars and Venus signs is unsettled, and the alchemical signs are attested in lists in Byzantine manuscripts and spread by early modern printed tables. Agrippa treats the 'seals and characters' that the stars stamp on natural things (De occulta philosophia I.33), the sixteen geomantic figures and the characters drawn from them (II.48, II.51), and reads the planet and zodiac signs as pictures made 'by a certain likeness' (II.52). The planet and zodiac signs have been in Unicode since its first version (the UCD Age property says 1.1, 1993), the Alchemical Symbols block since 6.0 (2010), and the sixteen geomantic figures since 17.0 (2025, U+1CEE0-U+1CEEF).

firstAttestation.work: Astronomical tables, almanacs and horoscopes on papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, edited as P. Oxy. 4133-4300a
firstAttestation.author: anonymous scribes and astronomers; ed. Alexander Jones (1999)
firstAttestation.date: Roman and late antique. Which dated papyrus carries the earliest planet sign was not established. Wikipedia's 'Planetary symbols', citing Jones, mentions the Saturn sign in papyri dated AD 376 and AD 481 (not seen).
firstAttestation.locator: A. Jones, Astronomical Papyri from Oxyrhynchus (Memoirs of the American Philosophical Society 233, 1999), vol. 1, pp. 62-63, as cited by Wikipedia's 'Planetary symbols'. Not seen in this check.
firstAttestation.notes: The earliest attestation named here, and only for the PLANET signs, and only on secondary report of Jones: Saturn and Jupiter as letter monograms (κρ, Ζ with an abbreviation stroke), Mercury as a caduceus-like sign; Mars and Venus unsettled. No papyrus was seen. ZODIAC glyphs: no early attestation was verified in any source named here (see claims). ALCHEMICAL sign lists: the earliest witness named here is Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, gr. Z. 299 (= coll. 584), dated by sources seen in search to the 10th century, to the end of the 10th or beginning of the 11th, or to c. 1000. Wikimedia Commons hosts the 1888 Berthelot-Ruelle reproductions of its lists of signs under the labels 'fol 6' and 'fol 7' (folio numbers not checked against the manuscript). Carlotta (2022) notes that such lists stand at the start or end of Byzantine alchemical collections. ELEMENT triangles: no source earlier than early modern printed tables was found.

transmission.date: Roman and late antique (dated papyri of AD 376 and 481 are cited for the Saturn sign; not seen)
transmission.author: anonymous; ed. A. Jones 1999
transmission.what: Planet signs used as shorthand in ephemerides and almanacs. As Wikipedia's 'Planetary symbols' reports Jones (1999, pp. 62-63): Saturn a monogram of κρ (Κρόνος) with an abbreviation stroke, Jupiter a Ζ (Ζεύς) with a horizontal stroke, Mercury a stylised caduceus; for Mars the papyrus form differs from the modern one and Jones implied but did not claim a monogram; in P. Oxy. 235 the Venus and Mercury signs lack the cross at the foot. Basis: secondary summary seen in search; Jones not seen.

transmission.date: 2nd c. CE (reported by Origen, mid-3rd c.)
transmission.work: Celsus, The True Word, quoted in Origen, Contra Celsum VI.22
transmission.author: Celsus; Origen
transmission.what: A Mithraic ladder of seven gates pairs metals with planets: lead with Kronos, tin with Aphrodite, bronze (copper) with Zeus, iron with Hermes, a mixed alloy with Ares, silver with the Moon, gold with the Sun. The sequence and pairings are confirmed in F. Crombie's translation (Ante-Nicene Fathers), as seen in search at bkv.unifr.ch; H. Chadwick's translation (Cambridge, 1953) exists but its wording was not seen.

transmission.work: Greek alchemical commentary ascribed to Olympiodorus (in Berthelot, Collection)
transmission.author: Olympiodorus (ascribed)
transmission.what: A commentary ascribed to Olympiodorus pairs electrum with Jupiter (Zeus) and tin with Mercury (Hermes), where the later standard pairs tin with Jupiter and quicksilver with Mercury. Confirmed only in a secondary source seen in search ('The Paradox of the Planetary Metals', ResearchGate); the page in Berthelot-Ruelle was not found.

transmission.date: 10th c., or late 10th/early 11th c., or c. 1000 (sources differ)
transmission.work: Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, gr. Z. 299 (= coll. 584)
transmission.author: anonymous Byzantine scribe(s)
transmission.what: The oldest and most important manuscript of the Greek alchemical corpus, base manuscript of Berthelot and Ruelle. It carries lists of signs for metals, minerals and other substances; Wikimedia Commons hosts Berthelot-Ruelle's 1888 reproductions of them labelled 'fol 6' and 'fol 7' (not checked against the manuscript). V. Carlotta (2022) studies its signs in Stephanus's Lessons and the Dialogue of the Philosophers and Cleopatra. Dating per Carlotta's chapter, an Italian thesis (Pausillo) and other sources seen in search.

transmission.work: Latin translations of Arabic geomancy (among them the Ars geomantiae of Hugh of Santalla)
transmission.author: Hugh of Santalla and other translators
transmission.what: Bring the sixteen dot figures of ʿilm al-raml into Latin. Hugh of Santalla (fl. c. 1145) translated an Ars geomantiae from Arabic in northern Spain (Quaestio 19, 2019, as seen in search); a DFG project describes the earliest codification as a series of 12th-century Latin treatises on unidentified Arabic antecedents. That the Latin names Via, Populus, etc. go back to these first translations was not verified (Charmasson 1980, not opened).

transmission.author: Theodoros Pelekanos of Corfu (colophon), finishing the copy in Crete
transmission.what: A late Byzantine copy of the alchemical corpus (first part = 'Corpus B'), finished in Crete in 1478 according to its colophon (place given as Chantaka/Chandax; R. Halleux says Herakleion), with a list of more than two hundred symbols (Carlotta 2022). Already in the Fontainebleau library catalogue of 1545. Sources: M. Martelli, 'Late Byzantine Alchemical Recipe Books', and Carlotta 2022, as seen in search.

transmission.author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
transmission.what: Agrippa's declamation against the arts and sciences, printed by Grapheus in 1530 (catalogue record; SEP). Chapter 13 treats geomancy: according to secondary accounts seen in search (Princeton geomancy pages; a reprinted introduction), it names earlier geomancies (Haly, Gerard of Cremona, Bartholomew of Parma, Tandinus) and says of Agrippa's own that it differs from them but is no less superstitious and lying. The Latin of the chapter was not seen.

transmission.author: Paracelsus (Theophrastus von Hohenheim)
transmission.what: Sets out the three principles (tria prima): sulphur, mercury and salt. The triad gives later tables their three 'principle' signs. The link between the Paramirum writings and the three principles is confirmed only in a catalogue summary seen in search; the dates c. 1530-1531 and 'printed after 1541' are NOT verified.

transmission.author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
transmission.what: I.33 (1651 English p. 65): every star stamps its seals and characters 'even in these inferiour things, viz. in Elements, in Stones, in Plants, in Animals, and their members', followed by a plate of the planets' 'Divine Letters' as chiromancers know them (p. 68). II.48 (pp. 309-310): the sixteen geomantic figures, 'as a middle betwixt Images and Characters', in a table giving each figure's element, planet and sign. II.51 (pp. 316-319): characters made by 'binding together the points' of each geomantic figure, with a table by planet. II.52 (p. 320): characters 'drawn from things themselves by a certain likeness', explaining the zodiac and planet signs (Saturn from a sickle, Jupiter from a sceptre, Mars from a dart, Venus from a mirror, Mercury from a caduceus, the Moon from her horns) and giving mixed characters for the four triplicities. Chapter numbers checked against the 1533 Latin (OCR of the Library of Congress copy: I.33 'Cap. XXXIII', II.48 'Caput XLVIII', II.51 'Caput LI', II.52) and the 1651 English (EEBO-TCP A26565). Book I had been printed alone in 1531 (Antwerp: Grapheus, February 1531; Paris: Wechel), per catalogue records seen in search. The printer of 1533 is unnamed (LoC: 's.n.'); Soter is attributed by other catalogues.

transmission.author: trans. J.F. (probably John French, 1616-1657, per the TCP record)
transmission.what: First English translation (London: R.W. for Gregory Moule, 1651). The four chapter titles quoted below are checked against its keyed text, EEBO-TCP A26565 (CC0), with page numbers from the TCP page markers.

transmission.work: Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy
transmission.author: trans. Robert Turner
transmission.what: Prints in English, with Turner's other translations, 'Of Geomancy' under Agrippa's name, the 'Magical Elements' (Heptameron) ascribed to Peter de Abano, an 'Astronomical Geomancy' that library catalogues (Wellcome) link to Gerard of Cremona, 'The Nature of Spirits' (Georg Pictorius) and the 'Arbatel'. Its table of the sixteen figures (EEBO-TCP A26563) gives the same dot patterns and planets as this file. All the ascriptions are reported, not proven.

transmission.author: Johann Christoph Sommerhoff
transmission.what: A Latin-German pharmaceutical-chemical lexicon whose title page announces appended 'Characteres Metallorum, Mineralium, Planetarum, Ponderum, aliarumque Rerum Chymicarum' (catalogue and title page as seen in search). Whether its table includes the element triangles was NOT verified.

transmission.author: Carl Linnaeus
transmission.what: First use of the Mars and Venus signs for male and female (parents of hybrids), according to W. T. Stearn, Taxon 11, no. 4 (1962), 109-113, as reported by secondary sources seen in search.

transmission.author: L.-B. Guyton de Morveau, A.-L. Lavoisier, C.-L. Berthollet, A.-F. de Fourcroy; new characters by J.-H. Hassenfratz and P.-A. Adet
transmission.what: The new chemical nomenclature, with a 'nouveau systême de caractères chimiques' by Hassenfratz and Adet (title page as catalogued by the Wellcome Collection and the Met), begins to replace the old alchemical characters. Dalton's circles (1808) and Berzelius's letters (1813-14) follow: those two dates were not re-checked.

transmission.author: M. Berthelot and Ch.-Ém. Ruelle
transmission.what: Edits the Greek alchemical corpus, chiefly from Marcianus gr. 299, and reproduces the Byzantine lists of signs. Usually cited as 3 volumes; one catalogue record seen in search counts 4, with the Introduction as volume 1.

transmission.work: Die Geheimsymbole der Chemie und Medicin des Mittelalters; Alchemistische und chemische Zeichen
transmission.author: G. W. Gessmann; F. Lüdy-Tenger
transmission.what: Modern compilations of the signs: G. W. Gessmann, Die Geheimsymbole der Chemie und Medicin des Mittelalters (Graz, 1899; Wellcome digitised copy); F. Lüdy-Tenger, Alchemistische und chemische Zeichen (Berlin, 1928), described in the Unicode alchemical proposals as some 3,695 signs and variants in 128 tables. Neither was opened.

transmission.author: Unicode Consortium
transmission.what: Planet signs (U+2609, U+263D-U+2647) and zodiac signs (U+2648-U+2653) in the Miscellaneous Symbols block. The UCD Age property gives 1.1 (checked locally, UCD 15.0), but Age was assigned retroactively and starts at 1.1. Wikipedia's block history lists 106 characters of the block (then 'Miscellaneous Dingbats') as already in Unicode 1.0.0 (1991); U+2600-2613 plus U+261A-266F make exactly 106, but no per-character 1.0 list was seen.

transmission.author: Unicode Consortium
transmission.what: Adds the Alchemical Symbols block, U+1F700-U+1F773 (116 characters). Checked in this session against the Unicode Character Database shipped with Python 3.11 (UCD 14.0) and Perl 5.38 (UCD 15.0).

transmission.author: Unicode Consortium
transmission.what: Adds U+1F774-U+1F776 (LOT OF FORTUNE, OCCULTATION, LUNAR ECLIPSE) and U+1F77B-U+1F77F (HAUMEA, MAKEMAKE, GONGGONG, QUAOAR, ORCUS) to the Alchemical Symbols block (Age checked locally in UCD 15.0; release September 2022 per the Unicode blog as seen in search).

transmission.author: Unicode Consortium
transmission.what: Encodes the sixteen geomantic figures, U+1CEE0 GEOMANTIC FIGURE POPULUS to U+1CEEF GEOMANTIC FIGURE VIA, in the Miscellaneous Symbols Supplement block (proposal L2/23-218; Unicode 17.0 code chart and block history as seen in search). The code points run in binary order (one point = 1, two points = 0, head row first). Also completes the Alchemical Symbols block with U+1F777-U+1F77A (asteroid 'form two' signs). Names checked against UCD 18.0 (unicodedata2 18.0.0) in this check.

claims.claim: The Saturn and Jupiter signs began as monograms of the planets' Greek names in Roman-period astronomical papyri.
claims.evidence: Jones's edition of the Oxyrhynchus astronomical papyri (1999, vol. 1, pp. 62-63), as summarised by Wikipedia's 'Planetary symbols': κρ for Κρόνος and Ζ for Ζεύς, each with an abbreviation stroke. Jones not seen; the monogram explanation of the Greek names is older (Salmasius, as Stearn 1962 reports it is weighed against the attributes theory; secondary report).

claims.claim: Letter-by-letter: Saturn from κρ (Κρόνος), Jupiter from Ζ (Ζεύς); Mercury a stylised caduceus; Mars and Venus unsettled.
claims.evidence: As Wikipedia reports Jones: Saturn and Jupiter monograms; Mercury a caduceus; for Mars Jones 'implied, but did not explicitly claim' a monogram, and the papyrus form may be a spear. The derivation of Venus from Φ (Φωσφόρος) appears in popular and blog writing, where it is also doubted; it was not found as Jones's reading. The earlier version of this claim gave Θοῦρος, Φωσφόρος and Στίλβων as Jones's readings: not supported, removed.

claims.claim: The signs picture the gods' attributes or the figures of the signs: for Agrippa, Saturn's sickle, Jupiter's sceptre, Mars's dart, the Sun's roundness, Venus's mirror, Mercury's caduceus, the Moon's horns; the ram's and bull's horns, the Scales' balance, the Archer's dart, and so on.
claims.evidence: Documented as Agrippa's reading in De occulta philosophia II.52 (1533; J.F. 1651, p. 320; Latin a falce, a sceptro, a dardo, a speculo, a caduceo, read from OCR of the LoC copy). As an account of ORIGIN it conflicts with the monogram reading of Saturn and Jupiter (Jones, as reported), though for Mercury the caduceus is also what Wikipedia reports from Jones. Maunder (1934) points to antecedents in Roman art of the planetary gods (as reported). The 'thunderbolt' for Jupiter and 'shield and spear' for Mars given earlier are not Agrippa's.

claims.claim: The crosses at the foot of Mercury and Venus, and on Saturn and Jupiter, are late additions to the signs.
claims.evidence: Reported by Wikipedia from Jones and Maunder: in P. Oxy. 235 the Venus and Mercury signs lack the cross; the 12th-century diagram of Johannes Kamateros lacks it; the cross-marks appear in the late 15th or early 16th century; Maunder (1934), as secondary sources report him, took them to be an attempt to give the signs of the pagan gods a Christian flavour (paraphrase; Maunder not read). Saturn's cross-bar is also reported as a later addition. Present the motive as Maunder's suggestion only.

claims.claim: The zodiac glyphs are as old as the planet signs.
claims.evidence: Not resolved. No scholarly source seen in this check dates the earliest zodiac glyphs; popular sources assert a papyrus origin without evidence. Neugebauer and Van Hoesen, Greek Horoscopes (MAPS 48, 1959) has a section 'Symbols' (catalogue contents) but was not opened. The statement that the pictorial glyphs are 'a feature of medieval manuscripts' was not verified. Derivations such as Capricorn from τρ (τράγος) and Virgo from ΠΑΡ (Παρθένος) are unproven. Agrippa II.52 reads the zodiac signs as pictures (horns, embracing, tail, ear of grain, balance, dart, waters, fishes).

claims.claim: Before late antiquity the pairing of metals and planets was not fixed.
claims.evidence: Celsus's Mithraic ladder in Origen, Contra Celsum VI.22 (confirmed in Crombie's ANF translation): tin to Aphrodite, bronze to Zeus, iron to Hermes, the alloy to Ares. A list ascribed to Olympiodorus gives electrum to Zeus and tin to Hermes (secondary source only). The later standard: lead-Saturn, tin-Jupiter, iron-Mars, gold-Sun, copper-Venus, quicksilver-Mercury, silver-Moon.
sources: Origen, Contra Celsum VI.22, trans. F. Crombie (ANF); trans. Chadwick 1953 (not seen)
The Paradox of the Planetary Metals (secondary)

claims.claim: Byzantine manuscripts of Greek alchemy carry lists of signs for metals, minerals and operations, the metals written with planet signs.
claims.evidence: Marcianus gr. Z. 299 (10th/11th c.) and Parisinus gr. 2327 (1478, more than two hundred signs); lists printed by Berthelot and Ruelle (1887-88). V. Carlotta, 'Translating Alchemical Practice into Symbols: Two Cases from Codex Marcianus graecus 299' (2022), notes that such lists commonly open or close Byzantine alchemical collections. Folios: Commons labels the Marcianus reproductions 'fol 6' and 'fol 7' (not checked).
sources: Martelli, Late Byzantine Alchemical Recipe Books

claims.claim: Alchemical signs were a secret code.
claims.evidence: They were mostly abbreviations, used in recipes, notebooks and pharmacy as the planet signs were in tables. That alchemical secrecy relied more on cover-names (Decknamen) than on the signs is ascribed to Principe 2013, but the passage was NOT found in this check. Carlotta (2022) argues the Byzantine signs carried operative information for readers.

claims.claim: The four element triangles are ancient.
claims.evidence: No ancient or medieval source for them was found. That they stand in Sommerhoff 1701 is NOT verified (the book has a table of characters). Agrippa II.52 gives 'mixed characters' for the fiery, earthly, airy and watery triplicities, but their shapes are gaps in the TCP text and illegible in the OCR; whether they are triangles must be checked on a scan. The hexagram reading cannot be dated here.

claims.claim: Paracelsus taught three principles, sulphur, mercury and salt, as the constituents of bodies.
claims.evidence: Generally reported (Pagel; Principe). Pagel's 2nd revised edition (Basel: Karger, 1982) confirmed in catalogues; the 1958 first edition and the Opus paramirum dates were not confirmed in this check.

claims.claim: Agrippa teaches that every star stamps its seal and character on the things under it (elements, stones, plants, animals and their members), and that these marks carry the star's virtue.
claims.evidence: De occulta philosophia I.33, 'Of the Seals, and Characters of Naturall things' (J.F. 1651, pp. 65-68; checked in EEBO-TCP A26565; Latin 'De signaculis & characteribus rerum naturalium. Cap. XXXIII.', LoC copy OCR). The chapter ends with a plate of the planets' 'Divine Letters' known to chiromancers (p. 68). This reports Agrippa's teaching, not its truth.

claims.claim: Agrippa places the geomantic figures between images and characters and assigns them to the planets in pairs.
claims.evidence: De occulta philosophia II.48 (J.F. 1651, pp. 309-310, table; checked in EEBO-TCP A26565; 1533 'Caput XLVIII'). Planets in the table: Via and Populus to the Moon; Fortuna maior and minor to the Sun; Acquisitio and Laetitia to Jupiter; Puer and Rubeus to Mars; Puella and Amissio to Venus; Coniunctio and Albus to Mercury; Carcer and Tristitia to Saturn; Caput and Cauda draconis to the Dragon's head and tail. The same planets stand in the 1655 'Of Geomancy' table (EEBO-TCP A26563). J.F. gives English names only, and renders Amissio as 'Acquisition / Comprehended without', a slip.

claims.claim: Agrippa shows how to make characters by joining the points of the geomantic figures, with a table.
claims.evidence: De occulta philosophia II.51 (1533 'Caput LI'; J.F. 1651, pp. 316-319): characters made 'binding together the points' of each figure, with a table by planet ('From the way', 'From the people', ... 'From loosing', ...) and characters of the Dragon's head and tail. The table's drawings are not transcribed in TCP and were not seen, so no character from it is described.

claims.claim: Agrippa wrote the treatise 'Of Geomancy' printed under his name.
claims.evidence: Printed in English by Turner (1655) and among Agrippa's works. Agrippa did write a geomancy: secondary accounts seen in search (Princeton geomancy pages) report that in 1526 he sent to Metz for his work on geomancy and that he refers to it again in De vanitate ch. 13, and judge it 'likely' to be the printed treatise. That identification is a scholar's inference, not proven. The Fourth Book printed with it is spurious (Weyer's testimony, as the Latin hall already says).

claims.claim: Gerard of Cremona wrote the 'Astronomical Geomancy'.
claims.evidence: So ascribed in print (Turner 1655); library catalogues (Wellcome) link the 'Astronomical geomancy' to Gherardo da Cremona. That Charmasson (1980) doubts the ascription was NOT verified in this check.

claims.claim: Geomancy reached Latin from Arabic ʿilm al-raml in the 12th century.
claims.evidence: Hugh of Santalla (fl. c. 1145) translated an Ars geomantiae from Arabic in 12th-century Spain, called the oldest Latin handbook of geomancy in a 2019 Quaestio article; a DFG project describes the earliest codification as a series of 12th-century Latin treatises based on unidentified Arabic antecedents (both as seen in search). Charmasson (Geneva: Droz, 1980) remains the standard study.

claims.claim: Geomancy was taught by the angel Gabriel (Jibril) to the prophet Idris, identified with Enoch or Hermes.
claims.evidence: The Arabic geomancers' own account, reported as legend. Seen only in Wikipedia's 'Arabic geomancy' (Idris taught by Jibril in a dream, the art then passing to an Indian king, Ṭumṭum al-Hindī). That Savage-Smith and Smith (1980) report it, and that Daniel is named as a recipient, were NOT confirmed; Daniel is removed from the claim.

claims.claim: Linnaeus first used the Mars and Venus signs for male and female.
claims.evidence: W. T. Stearn, 'The origin of the male and female symbols of biology', Taxon 11, no. 4 (May 1962), 109-113: first in the dissertation Plantae hybridae, 1751, for the female and male parents of hybrids; used freely in Species Plantarum (1753). Confirmed via secondary reports of Stearn (Wikipedia 'Gender symbol' and others).

claims.claim: Unicode has encoded the planet and zodiac signs from its first version (1.0, 1991; the UCD Age property says 1.1, 1993), the Alchemical Symbols from 6.0 (2010) with additions in 15.0 (2022) and 17.0 (2025), and the sixteen geomantic figures from 17.0 (2025).
claims.evidence: Code points, names and Age values checked locally (UCD 14.0, 15.0; names in UCD 18.0 via unicodedata2). Version 1.0 per the Miscellaneous Symbols block history; 17.0 per its code chart and the Unicode 17.0 release announcement (9 September 2025), as seen in search.
sources: Unicode code charts U+2600, U+1F700, U+1CEC0

claims.claim: The Unicode reference glyphs show the 'original' alchemical signs.
claims.evidence: The block encodes a selection of frequent signs in one chosen shape each; historical tables show many variants for the same substance. Lüdy-Tenger's catalogue counts some 3,695 signs and variants (Unicode alchemical proposals, as seen in search). The Noto renders made in this workflow show modern designs.

letters.name: Sun
letters.value: the Sun (Helios, Sol); in alchemy, gold
letters.form: One open circle, centre (50,50), radius 38. One solid dot at the centre, radius 6. Nothing else.
letters.note: Alchemy writes gold with this same sign. Unicode also has U+1F71A ALCHEMICAL SYMBOL FOR GOLD, whose Noto glyph adds a curling flourish to the circle; do not substitute it here. U+2609 is not in the Noto Sans Symbols 'symbols' subset probed in this session (it rendered as a missing glyph), which is one more reason to draw it.
letters.earliestForm: Wikipedia ('Astronomical symbols'; 'Solar symbol') reports a circle with a single ray for the Sun in the 12th-century astrological compendium of Johannes Kamateros and says the circle with a central dot first appears in the Renaissance; not checked against manuscripts. The earlier statement that the ray form is reported from the Oxyrhynchus papyri was not confirmed. Agrippa II.52 reads the Sun's character as made 'from roundness, and a golden brightness'.

letters.name: Moon
letters.value: the Moon (Selene, Luna); in alchemy, silver
letters.form: A crescent with its horns to the LEFT, bulging right like a closing bracket ')'. Horn tips at (40,10) and (40,90). Outer edge: an arc from tip to tip bulging right to x=78. Inner edge: a shallower arc from tip to tip bulging right to x=58. The crescent is about 20 units thick at mid-height and tapers to points. It may be filled; Noto draws it as an outline (both arcs stroked, hollow inside).
letters.note: Unicode has two crescents: U+263D FIRST QUARTER MOON (horns left, used here) and U+263E LAST QUARTER MOON (horns right). Alchemical silver is written with a crescent; U+1F71B ALCHEMICAL SYMBOL FOR SILVER has an unrelated Noto glyph (a ring with three small rings) and should not be used for the Moon.
letters.earliestForm: A crescent; no early form was checked. The direction of the horns varies between sources. Agrippa II.52 reads the Moon's character as made 'from her horns of increasing and decreasing'.

letters.name: Mercury
letters.value: the planet Mercury (Hermes, Stilbon); in alchemy, quicksilver and the principle Mercury
letters.form: Three parts on one vertical axis x=50. (1) Horns: a half circle open upward, centre (50,8), radius 15, so its tips are at (35,8) and (65,8) and its lowest point at (50,23). (2) A circle, centre (50,40), radius 17, touching the horns at (50,23). (3) Below the circle a stem from (50,57) to (50,96), crossed at y=80 by a bar from x=36 to x=64.
letters.note: Same sign serves for the alchemical metal quicksilver and for Mercury as one of the three principles (no. 25). Draw it once and reuse it.
letters.earliestForm: Wikipedia ('Planetary symbols'), citing Jones 1999, describes Mercury's sign in the papyri as a stylised caduceus; the derivation from Στίλβων given earlier was not found and is withdrawn. In P. Oxy. 235 (as reported) the sign lacks the cross at the foot. Agrippa II.52: 'from a Wand' (Latin a caduceo).

letters.name: Venus
letters.value: the planet Venus (Aphrodite, Phosphoros); in alchemy, copper
letters.form: A circle, centre (50,34), radius 24 (top at y=10, bottom at y=58). Below it a stem from (50,58) to (50,96), crossed at y=80 by a bar from x=34 to x=66.
letters.note: Unicode names this character FEMALE SIGN. Label it 'Venus' on the page. Its use for 'female' goes back to Linnaeus (see claims).
letters.earliestForm: Origin not established. A derivation from Φ (Φωσφόρος) is a proposal in popular writing, doubted there too, and was not found as Jones's reading; the hand-mirror reading is interpretation (Agrippa II.52: 'from a Lookinglass', Latin a speculo). In P. Oxy. 235 (as reported) the sign lacks the cross at the foot.

letters.name: Mars
letters.value: the planet Mars (Ares, Pyroeis); in alchemy, iron
letters.form: A circle, centre (38,62), radius 25. From the circle's upper right edge at 45 degrees (about (56,44)) a straight shaft runs up and right to (86,14). At its end a filled triangular arrowhead with its tip at (90,10) and its back corners at about (72,14) and (86,28). An open head of two short strokes from the tip, one horizontal and one vertical, is an accepted variant.
letters.note: Unicode names this character MALE SIGN. Label it 'Mars' on the page.
letters.earliestForm: Origin unsettled. As Wikipedia reports Jones, the papyrus form differs from the modern one (perhaps a spear) and Jones implied but did not claim a monogram; the Θοῦρος derivation given earlier was not found and is withdrawn. Agrippa II.52: 'from a bolt' (Latin a dardo, a dart). Shield-and-spear is a later reading.

letters.name: Jupiter
letters.value: the planet Jupiter (Zeus); in alchemy, tin
letters.form: Like an Arabic numeral 2 whose base runs on to the right and is cut by a tall upright. Upright: (72,10) to (72,92). Base bar: (20,68) to (72,68), meeting the upright, which stands above and below it. lettersSource: Not an alphabet. The 'letters' are the 51 units the page will show. Nos. 1-35 are Unicode-encoded signs: 7 planets, 12 zodiac signs, 4 elements, 3 principles (Mercury shares its sign with the planet), 5 substances (antimony, vitriol, sal ammoniac, aqua fortis, aqua regia) and 4 operations (sublimation, precipitation, distillation, putrefaction). Nos. 36-51 are the 16 geomantic figures, encoded since Unicode 17.0 (U+1CEE0-U+1CEEF). Each 'form' of nos. 1-35 describes the MODERN STANDARD shape, read off Noto Sans Symbols (@fontsource/noto-sans-symbols 5.3.0) on a 100-unit box, y downward; the fact-check compared every description with fresh Noto renders on a grid (tools_fc_signs2/img) and found them consistent. It is not traced from Agrippa, a manuscript or a papyrus. 'earliestForm' says what is known of the earliest shape; most of it rests on secondary reports, so no 'earliest form' variant should be drawn. The geomantic dot patterns follow the 1655 'Of Geomancy' table (EEBO-TCP A26563), not Agrippa's 1533 cut, which was not seen. uses.use: Engraving on talismans and in magical rites, as characters bearing the virtue of a planet or sign.
uses.evidence: Agrippa's teaching (I.33; II.48, where the geomantic figures 'engraven or imprinted under the dominion of their Planets and Signs, do conceive the vertue and power of images'; II.51; II.52), reported as his teaching; see also the planetary seals of II.22 (sibling item planetary-seals). Checked in EEBO-TCP A26565.

uses.use: Geomancy: four rows of points, made by marking dots at random and counting them, give a figure. Sixteen figures are combined in a chart and read for an answer.

links.relation: The Saturn and Jupiter signs are read as monograms of the Greek names Κρόνος and Ζεύς (Jones's reading, as reported); the Greek alchemical corpus carries the earliest lists of alchemical signs.
Same world: the astronomical papyri that carry the earliest planet signs come from Greek-writing Roman Egypt, where astrology and magic shared scribes and vocabulary.
Agrippa's Latin chapters on characters (I.33, II.48, II.51, II.52), the Latin geomantic names, and the Paracelsian tria prima.
Geomancy comes from Arabic ʿilm al-raml; Arabic alchemy carried the Greek signs and theory into Latin.
The Syriac alchemical corpus (Berthelot and Duval, 1893) is a bridge between Greek and Arabic alchemy.
Agrippa's 'characters of things' (I.33) and the characters drawn from geomantic figures (II.51) belong to the long practice of magical characters.
The planetary seals of II.22 ('Of the tables of the Planets ...', J.F. 1651) are a different set of signs from the planet signs shown here; do not confuse them.
Book III's angelic alphabets (III.29-30) are Agrippa's other kind of character; this page covers the signs of things, not of letters.

cautions: Checked in this fact-check: Agrippa's chapter numbers, titles and pages against the 1533 Latin (OCR of the Library of Congress copy) and the 1651 English (EEBO-TCP A26565); the geomantic dot patterns and planets against the II.48 table and the 1655 'Of Geomancy' table (EEBO-TCP A26563); every form description against fresh Noto renders; Unicode names and versions. Whatever is still marked 'not verified', 'as reported' or listed under factcheck.unresolved must not be printed as fact.

Every "form" of nos. 1-35 describes the modern standard shape (Noto Sans Symbols). Do not present any of these drawings as Agrippa's, a manuscript's or a papyrus's form. Label the plate "modern standard forms".
Do not draw an "earliest form" variant (papyrus Saturn, ray-Sun, etc.) from this file: none was seen.

The papyrus derivations rest on Wikipedia's summary of Jones 1999 (vol. 1, pp. 62-63). Only Saturn (κρ) and Jupiter (Ζ) may be given as Jones's monogram readings, and only as reported; do not give Θοῦρος, Φωσφόρος or Στίλβων as Jones's readings.

Agrippa's II.51 characters (table, J.F. 1651, pp. 317-319), the I.33 plate of the planets' 'Divine Letters' (J.F. 1651, p. 68), and the mixed, compound and fixed-star characters of II.52 are NOT described here. If the page shows them, trace them from a scan (1533: Library of Congress copy, loc.gov item 20007812).
Geomantic zodiac attributions are deliberately left out. They differ between Agrippa, the Gerard of Cremona geomancy and the Golden Dawn tables; do not present the Golden Dawn table as Agrippa's.
J.F.'s 1651 II.48 table gives English names only and renders Amissio as 'Acquisition / Comprehended without' (a slip; the Latin means loss). Use the Latin names on the page.
Unicode calls Venus FEMALE SIGN and Mars MALE SIGN, spells Scorpio SCORPIUS, Coniunctio CONJUNCTIO and Fortuna maior FORTUNA MAJOR. Use the planet, sign and Latin names on the page.

U+2648-U+2653 (zodiac) render as coloured emoji on most phones. Draw them as SVG, or add U+FE0E after each. Font support for the new geomantic code points (U+1CEE0-U+1CEEF, Unicode 17.0) was not checked: draw them as SVG.
U+1F71A GOLD and U+1F71B SILVER have unusual reference glyphs (a flourished sun; a ring with three small rings in Noto). Use the Sun and Moon signs for gold and silver, as the alchemists did.
U+1F70F BLACK SULFUR is the sign popularly called the "Leviathan cross", used today by a living organisation as an emblem. It is not shown here; if mentioned, do not reproduce it as an emblem.
Uranus, Neptune and Pluto (U+2645-U+2647) are modern signs and outside this page.
Maunder's suggestion that the crosses Christianised the signs is his suggestion, reported at second hand; present it as such or not at all.

factcheck.method: WebSearch (standard and extended) for every edition, date, shelfmark and attribution that could be searched; page fetching failed (no DNS), so URLs are only those that appeared in search results. Primary checks made directly: the EEBO-TCP keyed XML of the 1651 English Agrippa (A26565; I.33, II.22, II.48, II.51, II.52, with page-break markers) and of Turner's 1655 Fourth Book (A26563; the table of sixteen geomantic figures), and the OCR text of the 1533 Library of Congress copy (chapter heads and the Latin of II.52), all downloaded earlier in this workflow and read as data; Unicode names and Age values in UCD 14.0, 15.0 and 18.0 (unicodedata2 installed in an isolated folder); fresh Noto renders on a grid for every form description. The checker's own knowledge is used only to decide what to search, never as evidence.
corrections: summary: 'In Alexander Jones's reading ... the planet signs began as abbreviations of the planets' Greek names' overstated what could be found. Wikipedia's 'Planetary symbols' (citing Jones 1999, pp. 62-63) gives monograms only for Saturn (κρ) and Jupiter (Ζ), describes Mercury's sign as a stylised caduceus, and reports that Jones implied but did not claim a monogram for Mars; the Venus-Φωσφόρος derivation is a popular proposal.
